segments.title: Carrier design could lag behind carrier doctrine
segments.body: Aircraft-carrier doctrine could change during the years required to design and build a ship, turning a predicted white elephant into a useful carrier or an apparent ideal into a disappointment. Early construction also consumed treaty tonnage when institutional understanding was least mature. Conversions inherited compromises from the hull's original purpose and from how much construction had already been completed. A gunship's weight distribution, balance, and metacentric height were not designed for hangars and a flight deck.

evidence.note: Doctrine could change while a carrier was being built, reversing expectations about whether the completed ship would be useful.
Navies committed treaty tonnage to early carriers before they understood efficient carrier design.
Gunship conversions retained weight distributions and metacentric-height characteristics ill-suited to carrier operations.

segments.summary: Long construction times and compromised conversion hulls could leave a carrier embodying yesterday's doctrine by the time it entered service.

segments.title: Washington Treaty definitions and national carrier allowances
segments.body: The Washington Naval Treaty measured standard displacement with crew, ammunition, equipment, provisions, and drinking water aboard, but excluded fuel and reserve feed water. Its ordinary carrier limit was 27,000 tons, while cumulative allowances restricted how many ships each navy could build. Britain and the United States could each fit five carriers of that size into their allowance, and Japan three. France and Italy each had 60,000 tons, enough for two carriers at the maximum size or three of 20,000 tons. The 10,000-ton threshold left room for smaller carriers outside that accounting.

evidence.note: Washington Treaty standard displacement included crew, ammunition, and stores while excluding fuel and reserve feed water.
The 10,000-ton threshold, ordinary 27,000-ton carrier limit, and national cumulative allowances constrained carrier numbers and size.

segments.summary: Standard displacement, national tonnage allowances, and the 10,000-ton threshold shaped the number and size of carriers each navy could build.

segments.title: Battlecarriers had to justify combining two fleet roles
segments.body: The Washington Treaty allowed carrier guns up to eight inches, leaving room for cruiser armament while preventing a true battleship-carrier combination. That allowance reflected a period when guns were still more capable than aircraft and carrier roles remained unsettled. British battlecarrier proposals during the Second World War faced a practical objection: separate aircraft carriers and capital ships already supplied the proposed capabilities. Using a Lion-class hull for a hybrid also had to compete with completing it as a battleship. New light fleet and larger carrier programs provided another reason to question what operational need the hybrid would meet.

evidence.note: Eight-inch carrier armament limits and the British objection that separate carrier and capital-ship programs already met the proposed hybrid's needs.

segments.summary: Early carrier gun allowances reflected uncertain roles, while later British hybrids faced the question of what they added to separate carriers and capital ships.

segments.title: Lower flying-off decks and the cost of rebuilding British conversions
segments.body: Lower flying-off decks let British carriers launch fighters straight from the forward hangar when an attack appeared. Fighters could take off while torpedo aircraft remained ranged on the main deck, avoiding disruption to the strike group. Later proposals considered fitting an accelerator to keep the lower deck useful as aircraft developed. A more extensive rebuild would extend the main flight deck forward and enlarge the hangar, increasing capacity or preserving an air group of about 60 as aircraft grew. By the late 1930s the conversions were worn, and new carriers were entering service or construction. The suggestion that the Royal Navy had effectively abandoned the larger rebuild is an interpretation of those competing demands, rather than a stated formal decision.

evidence.note: Lower-deck fighter launches avoided disturbing a torpedo strike ranged on the main deck.
British accelerator terminology and proposals to fit a launch system on the lower flying-off deck.
A forward flight-deck and hangar extension could preserve aircraft capacity, but worn hulls and new construction weighed against rebuilding.

segments.summary: Rapid fighter launches gave the lower deck a purpose, while larger aircraft and worn hulls complicated plans to modernize Furious, Courageous, and Glorious.

segments.title: British conversions develop night flying for worldwide operations
segments.body: Furious, Courageous, and Glorious were already worn by heavy use when the Royal Navy considered their future in the late 1930s. They had helped develop carrier methods for the North Sea and North Atlantic as well as the Mediterranean and Far East. Britain needed doctrine that could work wherever its fleet deployed, which gave it different demands from a navy concentrated in one ocean. Night strikes and night flying were central to that work. Glorious conducted frequent night operations in the Mediterranean, while all three conversions contributed to the methods later carriers would inherit.

evidence.note: Hard-used British conversions supported doctrine intended for operations across several oceans.
Glorious's Mediterranean night operations and the contribution of all three conversions to night strikes and night flying.

segments.summary: Furious, Courageous, and Glorious helped develop night operations and carrier methods for Britain's commitments across several oceans.

segments.title: Japanese carrier experiments expose aircraft-growth risk
segments.body: Japan initially pursued large, fast carriers with multiple flying-off decks so aircraft could land above while fighters and strike aircraft launched from lower hangars. The arrangement promised rapid air-group operations but became less sustainable as aircraft grew larger. Akagi and Kaga initially combined stable hulls with lightweight hangar and flight-deck structures, which came under greater strain as aircraft grew heavier. Aircraft and carrier design had to develop together, with enough room for growth but without committing everything to a predicted future. Early ideas for Hermes included a stern ramp or telescoping crane to recover seaplanes that landed alongside, yet the Royal Navy hedged its bets instead of building exclusively around that concept. A seaplane-only Hermes is a counterfactual warning about excessive specialization. Hōshō faced the opposite limitation by the Second World War: newer aircraft were too heavy for her flight deck, restricting her to second-line training types.

evidence.note: Japan wanted fast, large carriers with multiple flying-off decks for rapid air-group operations.
Akagi and Kaga had lightweight structures that became more strained as aircraft grew heavier.
Early Hermes proposals included seaplane recovery by stern ramp or telescoping crane, but construction retained alternatives to an exclusively seaplane future.
By the Second World War, Hosho could operate only second-line training aircraft because newer types were too heavy for her flight deck.

segments.summary: Akagi, Kaga, Hosho, and Hermes illustrate how carrier layouts could age badly as aircraft became heavier and doctrine changed.

segments.title: Lexington and Ranger reverse early expectations
segments.body: Lexington and Saratoga were feared to be poor fits for the US Navy's developing carrier doctrine while they were under construction. Doubts included whether their decks would be long enough and whether they would have enough lifts. Ranger embodied expectations drawn from Sims's work and war gaming more closely, but experience with the conversions changed the understanding of what the doctrine required. By then Ranger's design was too far advanced to change readily. Lexington and Saratoga proved effective in service, and their operating experience became a stronger guide to the Yorktown class than Ranger's earlier design assumptions.

evidence.note: Lexington and Saratoga were expected to become white elephants before they were completed.
Deck length, lifts, Sims's war gaming, and practical experience changed expectations of Lexington, Saratoga, and Ranger and informed Yorktown.

segments.summary: The US Navy's supposed white elephants and ideal carrier design trade places once exercises and operations test the doctrine.

segments.title: Lexington's eight-inch guns and the case for escorts
segments.body: The objection to Lexington's eight-inch battery centers on placing heavy guns, armor, and supporting weight high on a carrier whose starboard island already created an imbalance. Before the London Treaty, the absence of a cumulative cruiser limit offered an alternative: build an escorting cruiser to handle surface threats. The preferred arrangement here is smaller dual-purpose guns about one deck below flight-deck level, where they retain useful firing arcs without adding as much topweight. Four-and-a-half-inch or five-inch mounts could engage aircraft and help repel destroyers that penetrated the escort. This is a design preference, and the criticism acknowledges that the US Navy had not yet developed the escort doctrine being proposed.

evidence.note: Criticism of the high eight-inch battery's weight and armor burden, with an escorting cruiser proposed instead.
Preference for smaller dual-purpose guns below flight-deck level, supported by cruisers and destroyers, with the absence of that doctrine acknowledged.

segments.summary: High-mounted heavy guns imposed a weight penalty; a preferred alternative combines lower dual-purpose mounts with cruiser and destroyer escorts.

segments.title: British operating evidence challenges the flush-deck carrier
segments.body: The US Bureau of Aeronautics remained attached to flush-deck carriers despite British operating experience that challenged the concept. An American naval attaché obtained reduced versions of Royal Navy reports through a senior British officer, with Admiralty permission. Britain was still exchanging information with the United States and Japan, so sharing the reports also served those relationships. Advocates nevertheless argued that American designers could avoid the British problems. Lexington and Saratoga provided another source of practical evidence by turning doctrine developed through war gaming into operations that could be applied across the fleet. Their experience helped shape the Yorktown design.

evidence.note: An American naval attaché obtained reduced British flush-deck operating reports with Admiralty permission during naval information exchanges.
Bureau of Aeronautics advocates could discount British operating experience by assuming that an American flush-deck carrier would avoid the same problems.
Lexington and Saratoga turned war-gamed doctrine into practical fleet operations and helped shape Yorktown.

segments.summary: The US Bureau of Aeronautics' attachment to flush-deck carriers illustrates how institutional preferences could resist allied operational evidence.

segments.title: London Treaty rules squeeze useful small carriers
segments.body: Britain's global commitments made small carriers attractive for convoy protection, trade nodes, and cruiser-carrier missions. Hermes and Argus had nevertheless shown that propulsion and other fixed requirements consumed a larger share of a small hull, leaving proportionally less space for aviation. More small carriers could cover several places at once, and losing one would remove a smaller share of the fleet's total aviation strength. Larger carriers offered greater aviation efficiency, so cumulative tonnage limits forced a choice between numbers and capability per hull. Lexington and Saratoga consumed so much of the US allowance that Ranger and Wasp became attempts to recover useful carrier numbers at lower displacement.

evidence.note: The London Treaty reflected greater understanding of naval aviation but discouraged useful small carriers.
Small carriers could suit Britain's global commitments, while larger carriers devoted proportionally more hull space to aviation.
Cumulative limits and the Lexington and Saratoga tonnage burden shaped the lower-displacement Ranger and Wasp designs.

segments.summary: Small carriers offered more hulls for global commitments, while larger carriers devoted a greater share of their displacement to aviation.

segments.title: The London Treaty closes the Ryūjō loophole
segments.body: The 1930 London Treaty redefined an aircraft carrier as a warship designed exclusively to carry aircraft that could take off from and land on it, regardless of displacement. Ordinary aircraft platforms on battleships, cruisers, and destroyers did not automatically make those ships carriers. The treaty also barred landing-on platforms or decks on capital ships already in existence on 1 April 1930. These rules closed the sub-10,000-ton route used for Ryūjō without solving navies' need for small carriers. A proposed alternative would give carriers of 15,000 tons and below a separate category and cumulative allowance, allowing small-carrier development within an agreed limit.

evidence.note: The London Treaty's revised aircraft-carrier definition closed the loophole under which Ryūjō and other Japanese small carriers could be built.
A proposed alternative gives fleet carriers and carriers of 15,000 tons and below separate cumulative allowances.

segments.summary: A revised carrier definition brings small Japanese designs such as Ryūjō inside treaty accounting, prompting a counterproposal for a distinct light-carrier category.

segments.title: A separate light-carrier allowance could reshape fleet roles
segments.body: A hypothetical light-carrier category would give Britain and the United States another 135,000 tons each, with proportional allowances of 81,000 tons for Japan and 60,000 tons each for France and Italy. The American force might include more Wasp-like ships, while a British design could resemble a lighter Unicorn or the later Colossus class. Nine British carriers of 15,000 tons could take over anti-submarine operations, reconnaissance, convoy protection, and fleet supply. They would absorb risks otherwise borne by Courageous and Ark Royal and could support forces such as Harwood's at the River Plate. Fleet carriers could then concentrate more closely on their own operational requirements, although the Royal Navy might still choose six smaller fleet carriers over five larger ones. Permitting limited Japanese small-carrier construction might also have softened resentment over the treaty's restrictions.

evidence.note: Proportional light-carrier allowances of 135,000, 81,000, and 60,000 tons could support Wasp-like American ships and British designs related to Unicorn or Colossus.
Limited permission for Japanese small-carrier construction might have reduced resentment over the treaty's restrictions.
Hypothetical British light carriers take anti-submarine, reconnaissance, convoy, and supply duties and could support Harwood at the River Plate.

segments.summary: A counterfactual light-carrier category shows how treaty architecture could distribute reconnaissance, convoy, anti-submarine, and fleet-support missions differently.

segments.title: Treaty limits raise a deterrence problem
segments.body: The criticism of the London Treaty here is that restricting possession of weapons did not necessarily reduce the risk of war. Preparedness can give governments confidence to set limits and resist intimidation. Credible warnings can make an aggressor back down, while fear and hesitation can weaken deterrence. In this interpretation, readiness and credible opposition to aggression offer a firmer basis for peace than nominal disarmament rules.

evidence.note: The London Treaty is criticized as reactionary because it seeks to prevent war by restricting possession of weapons.
Preparedness and confidence are advanced as reasons governments can manage conflict risk and make warnings credible.

segments.summary: The criticism of treaty disarmament rests on the view that readiness and credible warnings can deter aggression more effectively than nominal restrictions.

segments.title: Ranger exposes infrastructure and innovation limits
segments.body: Ranger translated Sims-era war gaming and Bureau of Aeronautics ideas into a purpose-built treaty carrier, but operational experience exposed the limits of the paper design. Her return from Pacific to Atlantic duty was partly an infrastructure decision: east-coast facilities could repair recurring problems more readily even though Atlantic seas were rougher. She still proved useful in operations such as Torch, but weight pressure and too many new ideas made her ill-suited to the highest-threat work. Flush-deck ambitions, unusual funnels, and the pressure to save weight concentrated too many untested ideas in one hull.

evidence.note: Ranger embodied Sims and Bureau of Aeronautics ideas; east-coast facilities made her recurring repairs easier to support, and she later served usefully in Operation Torch.
Ranger's weight-saving compromises reflected too many new ideas in one hull.

segments.summary: Ranger's recurring repairs favored Atlantic basing, where better infrastructure could maintain a carrier whose ambitious lightweight design caused operational problems.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth class tests the limits of design conservatism
segments.body: A naval design rule of thumb limits a new ship to about three major innovations; updated versions of familiar technology do not necessarily count as another major change. British dreadnought development separated changes in gun layout, gun type, propulsion, and speed across successive classes. On this reading, the Queen Elizabeth class had already used its allowance on 15-inch armament, layout, and higher speed, leaving newer small-tube oil-fired boilers outside the design. Those boilers might have helped the ships reach the intended speed, although the 1912-13 versions were less mature than those available in 1920. Adopting them is judged a reasonable additional risk in this case.

evidence.note: A design rule of thumb limits one ship to three major innovations, as successive British dreadnought changes illustrate.
Queen Elizabeth's armament, layout, and speed changes left small-tube oil-fired boilers outside the design despite their possible contribution to speed.

segments.summary: Limiting major innovations reduced design risk, but small-tube oil-fired boilers might have helped the Queen Elizabeth class reach its intended speed.

segments.title: Yorktown embodies the US alpha-strike doctrine
segments.body: The US Navy preferred large air groups because its doctrine sought to put the strongest possible first punch into the air, whether attacking or defending. A 40,000-ton amphibious assault ship such as the America class is too large to illustrate a preference for small carriers; the objection here concerns small air groups. Escort carriers answered the wartime need to spread aviation across more areas, even though large air groups remained the preference. Yorktown and Enterprise refined the lessons of Lexington, Saratoga, Ranger, and the interwar Fleet Problems into treaty carriers suited to that doctrine. Their more enclosed structure answered Ranger's torsional weakness, while lower gun positions and a hangar-deck catapult supported aviation without repeating Lexington's topweight. Exercises connected the intended doctrine to the arrangements needed to operate it.

evidence.note: The US Navy preferred large air groups and a first-punch doctrine for both offensive and defensive action.
Yorktown and Enterprise combined Fleet Problem experience with lower gun positions, a hangar-level catapult, and stronger structure than Ranger.

segments.summary: Large air groups, fast first punches, Fleet Problems, and conversion experience converge in the Yorktown-class design.

segments.title: Yorktown and Midway express doctrine, Essex emphasizes rapid construction
segments.body: Yorktown is judged closer to the US Navy's preferred carrier concept than the later Essex class. The Midway class takes that concept further by combining size, survivability, and aircraft capacity. Essex answers a different question: how large a carrier could be built quickly and in substantial numbers. Yorktown's priorities had already been refined through Lexington and Saratoga's exercises and the Fleet Problems.

evidence.note: Yorktown and Midway are judged close expressions of US carrier doctrine, while Essex emphasizes rapid construction in numbers.

segments.summary: Yorktown and Midway are judged closer to the preferred combination of size, protection, and air operations, while Essex answers the pressure to build quickly.

segments.title: Interwar carrier raids rehearse attacks on ships in harbor
segments.body: The US carrier raids of 1942 grew from interwar Fleet Problems that developed a raiding doctrine. American exercises twice used carriers to simulate successful attacks on Pearl Harbor. British planning also explored striking fleets that refused battle in port, informed in part by frustration with the German High Seas Fleet remaining in harbor during World War I. A fleet that stayed in port could still tie down the forces assigned to blockade it, giving the attacker another reason to strike inside the base. Moored ships could not maneuver and had restricted firing arcs amid other ships, fuel stores, and ammunition facilities. Pearl Harbor and the Battle of Taranto therefore fit a wider prewar search for ways to neutralize fleets inside defended bases.

evidence.note: The US Navy's 1942 carrier raids drew on interwar Fleet Problems that included two successful simulated attacks on Pearl Harbor.
Prewar exercises anticipated harbor attacks, while fleets remaining in port tied down enemy forces needed to blockade them.
Ships in port could not maneuver and had restricted firing arcs around other ships, fuel stores, and ammunition facilities.

segments.summary: US Fleet Problems and Royal Navy planning made harbor attack a rehearsed carrier mission well before Pearl Harbor and the Battle of Taranto.

segments.title: Sōryū and Hiryū test a paired-carrier island arrangement
segments.body: Japan explored paired-carrier operations by placing Hiryū's island to port while Sōryū retained the conventional starboard arrangement. Sailing with the islands adjacent could simplify communication between the ships while leaving the outer flight-deck edges open for aviation. The experiment challenged the safety logic behind the normal starboard island, which kept the structure away from the direction pilots were more likely to veer during a failed approach. Britain also considered coordinated carrier operations but avoided changing the layout in ways that would compromise landing safety. Japan's earlier carriers had consumed its 81,000-ton allowance, restricting construction while designers continued developing their ideas. Sōryū's 1935 launch and Hiryū's 1937 launch fell around Japan's withdrawal from the treaty system, linking this later construction to the removal of cumulative limits.

evidence.note: Opposite-side islands could simplify communication between paired Japanese carriers, while Britain avoided altering carrier layouts for the same concept.
Pilots' tendency to veer left during a failed approach favored starboard islands and made Hiryū's port-side island riskier.
Japan's earlier carriers consumed its 81,000-ton allowance, and Sōryū and Hiryū launched around withdrawal from the treaty system.

segments.summary: Opposite-side islands on Sōryū and Hiryū show Japan modifying ship design to support coordinated two-carrier operations.

segments.title: Ark Royal and Illustrious split British carrier priorities
segments.body: The Royal Navy expected its carriers to serve across several oceans and near hostile land-based aircraft. Treaty tonnage made it difficult to combine the desired strike group, continuous flying operations, and protection in enough hulls for those commitments. Ark Royal emphasized a large strike group while retaining more protection than many foreign designs. Tonnage savings nevertheless left weaknesses in her torpedo defenses, and her loss is linked here to a submarine torpedo, poor counter-flooding, and the stability characteristics of a tall double-hangar hull. Illustrious accepted a smaller strike group to give greater priority to protection and sustained flying. A larger Implacable-type carrier could bring those requirements together more fully.

evidence.note: The Royal Navy needed strike capacity, fleet survivability, and multi-theater reach but could not fit every desired quality into one treaty carrier.
Ark Royal's torpedo-defense compromises and tall double-hangar hull contributed to her loss after a submarine torpedo and poor counter-flooding.
British carriers emphasized continuous operations and combat air patrol, while US and Japanese carriers emphasized alpha strikes.
Implacable's larger design could combine alpha-strike capacity, continuous operations, and survivability.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy balances strike size, continuous air operations, and survivability by separating Ark Royal's role from the Illustrious-class armored carriers.

segments.title: British carriers sustain combat air patrol near enemy airfields
segments.body: British operations in the Mediterranean and South China Sea, including a planned blockade of Japan, would expose carriers to land-based aircraft. Reconnaissance spotters could provide visual early warning, but the practical requirement was to keep fighters airborne before a raid arrived. Carrier arrangements therefore had to support repeated launches of small strikes and fighter groups. Ark Royal combined a large strike group with continuous operations while falling short of the desired protection. Illustrious sacrificed some strike size to retain protection and sustained flying. At roughly 27,000 tons, an Implacable-type design could combine those capabilities more fully.

evidence.note: Operations near land-based aircraft, including a blockade of Japan, required continuous combat air patrol and experiments with visual early warning from reconnaissance aircraft.
Ark Royal and Illustrious made different compromises among strike size, continuous operations, and survivability, while an Implacable-type carrier could combine them.

segments.summary: Fighters needed to be airborne before land-based raids arrived, pushing British carrier design toward repeated sorties as well as large strikes.

segments.title: Wasp's deck-edge lift creates aviation space
segments.body: Wasp's deck-edge elevator preserved hangar and internal working space, helping a 14,900-ton carrier accommodate a large air group. Her more enclosed structure also made her a stronger design than Ranger. Both ships sacrificed speed: Ranger made 29.3 knots and Wasp 29.5, compared with Lexington's 34.5 and Yorktown's 32.5. The faster carriers had demonstrated the operational value of speed, which helped shape US doctrine. Deck-edge lifts and some deck parking might also have raised an Illustrious-class air group from roughly 36 to 48 aircraft, though that would have required changes elsewhere in the design. British doubts included memories of losing aircraft in the North Sea and concerns about survivability.

evidence.note: Wasp was the first carrier with a deck-edge lift; she displaced about 14,900 tons, carried up to 100 aircraft, and had three elevators and four catapults.
Ranger and Wasp both sacrificed speed, while Wasp's more enclosed structure and deck-edge lift improved structural strength and usable aviation space.
A hypothetical Illustrious design using deck-edge lifts and deck parking might accommodate about 48 aircraft instead of 36.

segments.summary: Wasp's deck-edge elevator shows how one arrangement could improve hangar space and air-group capacity within a constrained hull.

segments.title: The Second London Treaty frames the Illustrious compromise
segments.body: The Second London Naval Treaty removed cumulative carrier tonnage limits while imposing a nominal 23,000-ton limit per ship and a 6.1-inch gun ceiling. Its effectiveness depended on Japanese and Italian participation, since other navies would eventually have to respond if those countries ignored the restrictions. The exact declared displacements of Illustrious and the Lexington conversions invite skepticism about treaty accounting. Royal Navy studies considered carriers of up to 30,000 tons, then tested what capabilities could most safely be sacrificed to meet the limit. Illustrious retained protection against bomb damage and continuous sortie generation at the cost of a smaller air group. Deck-edge-lift options are less certain: Clarke had found notes suggesting their consideration but had not found the corresponding drawings.

evidence.note: The treaty lacked Japanese and Italian participation, set a 23,000-ton carrier limit and 6.1-inch gun ceiling, and removed cumulative limits.
The Illustrious class's exact 23,000-ton declaration and the Lexington class's exact 37,000-ton declaration invite skepticism about treaty accounting.
Royal Navy studies included carriers of up to 30,000 tons before cutting the capabilities most affordable to lose.
Illustrious prioritized damage resistance and sorties per aircraft. Notes suggested deck-edge-lift options, but Clarke had not found their drawings.

segments.summary: The nominal 23,000-ton limit and the Illustrious design studies show the Royal Navy deciding what capability it could most afford to sacrifice.

segments.title: Unicorn supplies the armored carrier air group
segments.body: The Illustrious class's smaller air group and emphasis on sortie generation left less room for spare aircraft and major maintenance. Damaged aircraft requiring substantial work had to move elsewhere so the carrier could continue operating its air group. Mediterranean bases such as Alexandria and Malta could provide repair facilities and replacements, but the Far East presented a different support problem. HMS Unicorn carried that maintenance and replacement capacity forward with the fleet. Her role allowed protected fleet carriers to concentrate on flying operations without accommodating every support function themselves.

evidence.note: Armoured carriers needed external spare-aircraft and major-maintenance support, available from Mediterranean bases but requiring a forward support ship in the Far East.

segments.summary: HMS Unicorn restores spare-aircraft and major-maintenance capacity that armored fleet carriers sacrificed for protection and sortie generation.

segments.title: Unicorn's maintenance role and the treaty's auxiliary category
segments.body: The Second London Treaty restricted auxiliaries to 28 knots, barred guns larger than 6.1 inches, and permitted no more than eight guns larger than 3 inches. Its definition also excluded torpedo armament, armor protection, and ships designed primarily to operate aircraft at sea. Unicorn's original design included a structure in the middle of the flight deck, consistent with her designation as a forward aviation maintenance ship. Her 24-knot speed, eight 4-inch guns, and lack of torpedoes fitted those particular auxiliary limits. Construction changes removed the central obstruction, and the completed ship carried limited armor on the flight deck and around the magazines, so the original classification needs to be distinguished from the ship as completed. Unicorn came from the same design study as Illustrious and became a template for later light fleet carriers.

evidence.note: The auxiliary definition restricted armament, speed, protection, torpedoes, and aircraft operation.

Unicorn's original maintenance layout and specifications differed from the completed ship, which lost the central deck obstruction and carried limited armor. Her design shared the Illustrious study and influenced light fleet carriers.

segments.summary: Unicorn's initial maintenance layout supported an auxiliary classification, while construction changes produced a more capable aviation ship.

segments.title: Larger carrier allowances could reduce design compromises
segments.body: British, American, and Japanese carrier designers all wanted large strikes, continuous operations, and survivability. Treaty limits forced each navy to sacrifice capabilities according to its own doctrine and priorities. One counterfactual removes cumulative carrier limits while retaining the Washington Treaty's 27,000-ton limit per ship. Another gives carriers an allowance comparable with capital ships, such as fifteen carriers alongside fifteen capital ships. Either change would permit larger carrier forces and reduce the pressure to divide a small allowance among hulls that could not combine all the desired capabilities.

evidence.note: Shared operational goals underpin counterfactual proposals to remove or greatly increase cumulative allowances while retaining a 27,000-ton unit limit.

segments.summary: Removing or greatly increasing cumulative allowances could let navies build carriers that combined more of their shared operational requirements.

segments.title: A light-carrier category invites wider changes to treaty limits
segments.body: A distinct light-carrier category could let larger fleet carriers concentrate on the duties for which they were designed. The same approach could create clearer divisions among other warship types. One suggested arrangement allows 15,000-ton light carriers and heavy cruisers, 9,000-ton light cruisers, and 3,000-ton destroyers. A smaller capital-ship category is another possibility. Such rules might produce a more equitable agreement, though that depends on negotiators accepting something beyond immediate national advantage.

evidence.note: A hypothetical light-carrier category leads to proposed 15,000-ton heavy cruisers, 9,000-ton light cruisers, 3,000-ton destroyers, and a possible smaller capital-ship category, with doubts about diplomatic agreement.

segments.summary: Separate light-carrier allowances could accompany more widely spaced cruiser and destroyer limits, though the diplomatic outcome remains uncertain.

segments.title: An early treaty collapse could permit a larger British carrier
segments.body: If Japan and Italy had left the treaty system at the 1930 London conference, carrier construction in the mid-1930s might have faced fewer restrictions. The likely British design in this counterfactual resembles an Implacable with Ark Royal-sized hangars. It combines protection for operations near enemy airfields with a substantial strike group and a second hangar for maintenance. That arrangement could remove the need for a separate Unicorn-type support ship. Because the major carrier navies wanted many of the same capabilities, greater design freedom might have brought their ships closer together.

evidence.note: An imagined 1930 treaty collapse permits a British carrier combining Implacable's protection with Ark Royal-sized hangars and its own maintenance capacity, supporting the prediction of design convergence.

segments.summary: An imagined treaty collapse in 1930 permits a British carrier with Implacable's protection, Ark Royal-sized hangars, and extensive maintenance facilities.
